deep.reconstruction:
This page is the opening of Section 7, the start of the main part of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (written 1854, published posthumously by Dedekind in 1867). The section is titled 'Untersuchung der Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe ohne besondere Voraussetzungen über die Natur der Function'.

There is no computation on the page. It contains (i) a statement of programme and (ii) the definition of notation.

(i) Programme. Earlier work (Fourier, Dirichlet and others) aimed to justify the Fourier series for the cases that occur in nature. Such work could therefore start from an arbitrary function and later impose convenient restrictions, provided these did not defeat that aim. Riemann's aim is different: only the conditions *necessary* for representability may be imposed. So he must first find necessary conditions and then pick sufficient ones from among them. Earlier work proved implications of the form 'if f has properties P, then its Fourier series represents it'. Riemann reverses the question: 'if a function is represented by a trigonometric series, what follows about its behaviour, i.e. how its value changes as the argument changes continuously?' This is the conceptual shift from Fourier series to general trigonometric series, where the coefficients are not assumed to be Fourier coefficients of an integrable function.

(ii) Notation. He considers the formal series
 a_1 sin x + a_2 sin 2x + ... + (1/2) b_0 + b_1 cos x + b_2 cos 2x + ...
and abbreviates
 A_0 = b_0/2, A_n = a_n sin(nx) + b_n cos(nx) for n >= 1,
so the series becomes A_0 + A_1 + A_2 + ...

The next page names this series Omega and its sum f(x), defined only where the series converges. That page then begins Section 8 with the twice term-wise integrated series F(x) = C + C'x + A_0 x^2/2 - sum A_n/n^2. This is the starting point of Riemann's second-symmetric-derivative method; it does not appear on this page.

results.what: Methodological inversion: study arbitrary trigonometric series and ask what representability implies (necessary conditions), rather than proving that Fourier series converge under sufficient conditions.
results.modern_name: Theory of general (non-Fourier) trigonometric series; uniqueness/representation problem

results.what: Notation A_0 = b_0/2, A_n = a_n sin nx + b_n cos nx for a general trigonometric series
results.modern_name: Standard real form of a trigonometric series
results.usually_credited_to: Standard (Euler/Fourier tradition); this exact notation is Riemann 1854

deep.surprise_reason: This is the manuscript of the well-known, published Section 7 of Riemann's 1854 Habilitationsschrift on trigonometric series. The text agrees with the printed version, and the programmatic statement is famous and long credited to him.

checkable.sympy: simplify(integrate(integrate(a*sin(n*x)+b*cos(n*x),(x,0,x)),x) - (-(a*sin(n*x)+b*cos(n*x))/n**2 + a*x/n)) (with n positive integer; equality up to linear terms C + C'x)
checkable.asserts: Twice integrating A_n gives -A_n/n^2 up to a linear function; context for the next page's F(x).
Twice integrating the constant term A_0 gives A_0 x^2/2.
A_n can be written as an amplitude times a phase-shifted sine, so A_n -> 0 for all x iff a_n^2+b_n^2 -> 0 (relevant to the next page's case split).

transcription_corrections: Transcription agrees with the image and with the published text; no substantive corrections. The '27.' at top right is the manuscript page number. The marginal '18' is the folio number and is not part of the text.
